blocks.content: Imagine you have been handed a task build an online food delivery app from scratch. Before a single line of code is written, before any database is designed, one question needs answering first:
"What is this system actually supposed to do?"
You need to see the system through the eyes of the people who will use it.
That is exactly what Use Case Diagrams are for.
They do not care about code. They do not care about databases or APIs. They simply capture who interacts with the system and what those people need it to do nothing more, nothing less.
In this chapter we will cover:
["What a Use Case Diagram is","The building blocks that make one up","How to draw one from scratch, step by step"]
items: What a Use Case Diagram is
The building blocks that make one up
How to draw one from scratch, step by step

blocks.content: 1. What is a Use Case Diagram?
blocks.text: 1. What is a Use Case Diagram?

blocks.content: A use case diagram is a behavioral UML diagram that shows who interacts with your system and what they can do with it.
Think of it as a menu for your system. Not how the kitchen prepares the food just what is available to order and who is allowed to order it.
It answers one simple question: "Who does what with this system?"

Notice what it does not answer. It does not touch implementation, class design, database structure, or any technical detail whatsoever. A use case diagram lives purely at the requirements level it captures scope and user goals and stops right there.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245791788-785bf596.png

Use case diagrams are typically created early right after requirements are gathered and before any detailed design begins. They act as a bridge between what the business needs and what the development team will build.

Interview Tip In LLD interviews you rarely need to draw a formal use case diagram on the spot. But taking sixty seconds to list out the actors and what each one needs to do before jumping into classes signals structured thinking and stops you from missing key requirements halfway through your design.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: 2. Building Blocks of a Use Case Diagram
blocks.text: 2. Building Blocks of a Use Case Diagram

blocks.content: A use case diagram has four building blocks: actors, use cases, the system boundary, and relationships. Simple on their own powerful when combined.
1. Actors

An actor is anything that lives outside the system and interacts with it. Usually a person a customer, an admin, a driver but it can also be an external system like a payment gateway or a notification service.
Actors come in two types and where you place them matters:
Primary actors kick things off. They have a goal and they come to the system to achieve it. A customer placing an order is a primary actor. Draw them on the left.

Secondary actors get called upon. The system reaches out to them during a use case. A payment gateway does not decide to charge someone on its own the system calls it during checkout. Draw them on the right.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245791923-8c8cee21.png
2. Use Cases
A use case is a specific goal the system helps an actor accomplish. It represents a complete interaction something that starts, does something meaningful, and ends with a result.
Three rules for writing good use cases:

["Start with a verb. Write \"Place Order\" not \"Order Placement.\" The verb keeps it action-focused.","Represent a complete goal. \"Place Order\" is a full goal. \"Click the submit button\" is a single step too small.","End with a meaningful result. After \"Place Order\" completes, the customer has a confirmed order. That is a real outcome."]
items: Start with a verb. Write "Place Order" not "Order Placement." The verb keeps it action-focused.
Represent a complete goal. "Place Order" is a full goal. "Click the submit button" is a single step too small.
End with a meaningful result. After "Place Order" completes, the customer has a confirmed order. That is a real outcome.

blocks.content: 3. System Boundary
The system boundary is a rectangle that wraps around all the use cases. It draws a clear line between what your system does and what lives outside it. The system name sits at the top.
Actors always sit outside the box. Use cases always sit inside.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245792013-874c24c2.png
4. Relationships
Relationships are the lines that connect actors to use cases and use cases to each other. There are four types.
a. Association
A solid line between an actor and a use case. It simply means this actor takes part in this use case. The most common line you will draw.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245792166-e44ad99f.png
b. Include
One use case always triggers another as a required step. The base cannot finish without it. The arrow points from the base use case to the one it pulls in, labeled <>.
"Place Order" always includes "Process Payment." There is no order without a payment. Every single time, no exceptions.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245792246-4cee4839.png
c. Extend

One use case optionally adds extra behavior to another under certain conditions. The base use case runs perfectly fine on its own. The arrow points from the optional use case back to the base, labeled <>.
"Apply Promo Code" extends "Place Order." Most customers just order without a code. But when they have one, the option is there. The base use case never changes.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245792498-c7be13b0.png
d. Generalization

Inheritance between actors or between use cases. A child actor inherits every use case the parent has access to, and can have additional ones of their own. The arrow points from child to parent with a hollow triangle tip.
An Admin is also a User. They can do everything a regular user can browse items, place orders but they can also manage the entire platform on top of that.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245792586-e5af4e75.png
3. How to Draw a Use Case Diagram (Step by Step)
blocks.text: 3. How to Draw a Use Case Diagram (Step by Step)

blocks.content: Let's build a use case diagram from scratch for an Online Food Delivery App. We will go one step at a time and finish with a complete diagram.
Step 1: Identify the Actors
Ask yourself who or what interacts with this system from the outside?

["Customer (primary) places orders, tracks deliveries","Restaurant Owner (primary) manages menu and incoming orders","Delivery Driver (primary) picks up and delivers orders","Payment Gateway (secondary) gets called by the system during checkout"]
items: Customer (primary) places orders, tracks deliveries
Restaurant Owner (primary) manages menu and incoming orders
Delivery Driver (primary) picks up and delivers orders
Payment Gateway (secondary) gets called by the system during checkout

blocks.content: Step 2: List the Use Cases
Now ask what does each actor actually want to accomplish?

["Customer: Browse Restaurants, Place Order, Track Order, Cancel Order, Leave Review","Restaurant Owner: Manage Menu, Accept Order, View Earnings","Delivery Driver: Accept Delivery, Update Delivery Status","System level: Process Payment (triggered during Place Order)"]
items: Customer: Browse Restaurants, Place Order, Track Order, Cancel Order, Leave Review
Restaurant Owner: Manage Menu, Accept Order, View Earnings
Delivery Driver: Accept Delivery, Update Delivery Status
System level: Process Payment (triggered during Place Order)

blocks.content: Step 3: Define the System Boundary
Draw a box around all the use cases and label it. Everything inside is what your system builds and owns. Everything outside the actors is external.
Step 4: Draw Associations
Connect each actor to the use cases they take part in with solid lines.

["Customer connects to Browse Restaurants, Place Order, Track Order, Cancel Order, Leave Review","Restaurant Owner connects to Manage Menu, Accept Order, View Earnings","Delivery Driver connects to Accept Delivery, Update Delivery Status","Payment Gateway connects to Process Payment"]
items: Customer connects to Browse Restaurants, Place Order, Track Order, Cancel Order, Leave Review
Restaurant Owner connects to Manage Menu, Accept Order, View Earnings
Delivery Driver connects to Accept Delivery, Update Delivery Status
Payment Gateway connects to Process Payment

blocks.content: Step 5: Add Include, Extend and Generalization
blocks.text: Step 5: Add Include, Extend and Generalization

blocks.content: Look for mandatory steps and optional additions.

["Place Order <> Process Payment every order must go through payment, no exceptions","Place Order <> Apply Promo Code customers can optionally apply a discount code","Premium Customer generalizes Customer a premium customer can do everything a regular customer can, plus access exclusive deals"]
items: Place Order <> Process Payment every order must go through payment, no exceptions
Place Order <> Apply Promo Code customers can optionally apply a discount code
Premium Customer generalizes Customer a premium customer can do everything a regular customer can, plus access exclusive deals

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245792691-e8f3ba7a.png
Reading the Diagram

["Green nodes on the outside are actors they live outside the system boundary","Blue nodes inside the box are use cases things the system provides","Red node is the optional extending use case","Yellow node is the secondary actor called by the system, never initiates","Solid lines are associations, dashed labeled arrows show include and extend, and the hollow arrow shows generalization"]
items: Green nodes on the outside are actors they live outside the system boundary
Blue nodes inside the box are use cases things the system provides
Red node is the optional extending use case
Yellow node is the secondary actor called by the system, never initiates
Solid lines are associations, dashed labeled arrows show include and extend, and the hollow arrow shows generalization
